chunks: How timers work and are implemented. The question: How do they work? How are they implemented?
Inside the chip, a timer is a row of flip-flops that counts in binary, plus a small circuit that checks whether the count equals a stored number.
A flip-flop is a one-bit memory that updates on each clock tick. When the count matches, the hardware sets a flag (a status bit).
That flag can signal the processor, flip a pin, or send the counter back to zero.
Think of a car's odometer. Each digit wheel advances one step when the wheel to its right rolls past 9.
A binary timer works the same way, but each wheel has only two positions, 0 and 1. Now add an alarm that rings when the odometer shows a chosen number, and resets it to zero.

Flip-flop: a one-bit memory that copies its input when the clock ticks. Counter: flip-flops that each flip when all the lower bits are 1, so together they count up in binary.
Comparator: logic that checks whether two numbers are equal, bit by bit. Prescaler: a small counter that lets the main counter advance only once every N clock ticks.
Take a 3-bit counter. Bit 0 toggles on every tick, bit 1 on every second tick, and bit 2 on every fourth. Together they count 0, 1, 2, up to 7, then wrap. That is 8 states, not 7.
Now a real timer: a 16 megahertz clock and a prescaler that emits a pulse every 16th tick make the counter advance at 1 megahertz. A reload value of 999 is stored.
When the count equals 999, the next tick loads 0 instead of adding 1. That makes 1000 states per period, so 1 kilohertz. That is the whole idea.

"A timer is a synchronous binary counter made of flip-flops with an incrementer, a prescaler that is itself a small counter giving an enable pulse every N clocks, and comparators that check the count against a value in a register.
A match sets a flag that can interrupt, toggle a pin, or reload the counter.
For input capture, an external edge goes through a synchroniser and loads the count into a capture register.
The CPU just accesses all of it as memory-mapped registers, often with shadow registers so changes apply cleanly at the next period."
